intro_script: Welcome to your daily research digest for October 31st, 2026. Today we cover breakthroughs in AI agent environments, memory-efficient machine learning, and the future of knowledge graphs.
outro_script: And that's all for your daily dive into research! From the wild web to scalable agents, keep exploring those connections. Thanks for tuning in; happy researching!

items.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
items.summary: WebAnything is a framework designed to reconstruct source-grounded, reusable web environments from URLs without manual site implementation. It utilizes an Explorer-Builder to collect observable structures and interaction outcomes, along with an independent verifier for local repair or source recapture. The system successfully constructs 244 website artifacts across various domains and supports numerous executed tasks. Compared to human-assisted methods, WebAnything achieves superior scores on fidelity metrics. Fine-tuning a large language model on interaction trajectories further improves overall success in related agent tasks.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments" details a framework designed to reconstruct source-grounded, reusable web environments from URLs without manual site implementation, achieving the construction of two hundred forty-four website artifacts across various domains. The system employs an Explorer-Builder to collect observable structures and interaction outcomes, augmented by an independent verifier intended for local repair or source recapture. This process successfully constructs artifacts and supports numerous executed tasks, demonstrating superior fidelity scores when compared against human-assisted methods. Further success in related agent tasks is achieved through fine-tuning a large language model on the collected interaction trajectories. This advancement suggests a pathway toward scalable and automated creation of complex digital environments through agentic systems.

items.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.summary: LRMoE is a memory-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training system designed for memory-constrained nodes. It jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload during training. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints. During backpropagation, it estimates token-expert contributions and distributes retained pairs across experts. Experiments demonstrate that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time by 21.2-44.8% compared to SYMI.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes" details a memory-aware Mixture-of-Experts training system that achieves significant reductions in training time. The research introduces LRMoE, a method designed for memory-constrained nodes by jointly recalibrating backward demand and balancing the retained workload during training. During the forward execution phase, the system plans retention quotas and expert placement while adhering to resource limitations. Subsequently, during backpropagation, LRMoE estimates token-expert contributions and distributes these retained pairs across the available experts. Experimental results indicate that this methodology reduces the cumulative MoE-layer training time by twenty-one point two to forty-four point eight percent when compared to existing methods. This advancement suggests a pathway toward more efficient and scalable training of large-scale Mixture-of-Experts models on current hardware.

items.title: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: LLM agents querying knowledge graphs are increasingly checked by ontologies, but these checkers may introduce errors or false alarms. The study investigates the performance of curated, LLM-generated, and data-derived ontologies used as checks over agent answers. The research compares the performance of these different ontology sources when checking agents across public and private knowledge graphs. Findings show that a curated ontology on UniProt flagged more correct answers than data-derived or LLM-derived ones. The study analyzes the trade-offs between catching errors and false alarms when using these ontologies as feedback for LLM agents.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs". This research investigates the performance of different ontology sources used to check answers from large language model agents querying knowledge graphs. The study compared curated, LLM-generated, and data-derived ontologies as checks over agent responses when querying both public and private knowledge graphs. The findings indicated that a curated ontology based on UniProt flagged more correct answers compared to the data-derived or LLM-derived alternatives. The research analyzed the balance between detecting errors and generating false alarms when employing these ontological checks as feedback mechanisms for the agents. This research suggests that the quality of the ontology significantly impacts the accuracy of LLM agent validation. Future work should focus on refining methods for generating high-quality ontological feedback for autonomous agents.

items.title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
items.summary: A document-grounded benchmark called LibStructBench was introduced to evaluate AI agents' ability to reconstruct sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Experiments revealed that frontier agents often achieve approximate, but not exact, reconstructions of protocol details like molecular states and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model had a significant impact on performance, especially for molecular-state reconstruction. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples did not yield mean improvements in the tested trajectory. These results emphasize the need for more verifiable approaches in AI reasoning about complex molecular experimental protocols.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding" details the introduction of a benchmark designed to evaluate artificial intelligence agents' capacity to reconstruct sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Experiments utilizing this benchmark indicated that frontier agents frequently achieve approximate, rather than exact, reconstructions of protocol details such as molecular states and workflow connectivity. The research involved testing the agents' performance across various protocol understanding tasks, observing the impact of switching the underlying language model on reconstruction accuracy, particularly concerning molecular-state reconstruction. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples did not result in mean improvements across the tested trajectories. This research underscores the necessity for more verifiable methodologies in artificial intelligence reasoning concerning intricate molecular experimental protocols. The findings suggest a growing requirement for verifiable methods in AI when interpreting complex scientific workflows.

items.title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.summary: ThinkJev addresses errors in typed decisions by allowing a single open hybrid-thinking model to generate answers either directly or after a thought process. It employs two systems, System 1 for direct answers and System 2 for answers after the model thinks, ensuring both operate on the same options. The system calibrates the thinking budget based on statistical tests to avoid unnecessary computation, achieving good accuracy without full deliberation. For instance, one system achieved 3.9% error on 8359 test decisions with a 5% target error rate. This approach allows for efficient, calibrated decision-making in language model outputs.

items.title: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback
items.summary: Seq@K is a new evaluation protocol designed to measure how language models use sequential feedback during problem-solving attempts. Unlike existing metrics like Pass@K, Seq@K specifically evaluates the model's ability to refine an answer across K sequential attempts with feedback after each failure. Evaluation on 7 benchmarks and 16 models showed that Seq@K reveals a different model-selection landscape than Pass@K. Analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behaviors, such as how quickly models address feedback. These results suggest that practitioners need to consider Seq@K for faithfully benchmarking language models operating in feedback-driven agentic workflows.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback" details a new evaluation protocol for measuring how language models utilize sequential feedback during problem-solving attempts. The protocol specifically evaluates a model's capacity to refine an answer across K sequential attempts, incorporating feedback after each failure. Analysis of model trajectories under this framework allows for the characterization of iterative refinement behaviors, examining the speed with which models address received feedback. These findings indicate that considering Seq@K is necessary for accurately benchmarking language models operating within feedback-driven agentic workflows. This research provides a new methodology for assessing the iterative reasoning capabilities of large language models.

items.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
items.summary: Model discrepancy necessitates accounting for uncertainties in observations and contexts when calibrating a single model parameter. The method constructs localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods based on their proximity to a target context, incorporating context uncertainty via covariance inflation. A conditional normalizing flow approximates these localized posteriors using amortized variational inference. Applying this to an ocean turbulence closure reduces predictive errors for temperature and zonal-velocity relative to global calibration.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure" reports a method for model calibration that accounts for observational uncertainties within a specific context. The research details a method that constructs localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods based on proximity to a target context while incorporating context uncertainty through covariance inflation. A conditional normalizing flow is then employed to approximate these localized posteriors using amortized variational inference. This technique was applied to an ocean turbulence closure, resulting in a reduction of predictive errors for temperature and zonal-velocity relative to global calibration. The findings indicate a new approach for refining model parameters by integrating contextual uncertainty directly into the inference process. This work suggests a path toward more accurate physical modeling in complex systems.

items.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
items.summary: OpenFrontiers is a cross-disciplinary resource combining open research problems with a benchmark of recently resolved mathematical problems. It contains a corpus of 12,151 problems with associated information and a benchmark of 200 problems with resolution status. The evaluation protocol grades formal proofs using independent checkers in various conditions. Testing LLM agents on a subset reveals that closed-book rediscovery is rare, with success often correlating to retrieving published solutions. Ultimately, OpenFrontiers establishes a foundation for measuring research-level scientific rediscovery.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery" details a cross-disciplinary resource combining open research problems with a benchmark of recently resolved mathematical problems, establishing a foundation for measuring scientific rediscovery. The collection comprises twelve thousand one hundred fifty one problems with associated information alongside a benchmark of two hundred problems indicating resolution status. The evaluation protocol assesses formal proofs using independent checkers across various conditions. Testing large language model agents on a subset of this material indicated that closed-book rediscovery is infrequent, with success typically correlating to the retrieval of published solutions. This work ultimately sets a framework for quantifying research-level scientific rediscovery in artificial intelligence systems. The findings suggest a pathway for assessing the true capacity of AI in scientific discovery.

items.title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
items.summary: AI agents writing smart contracts often fail to capture the intended behavior, which is critical due to the immutable nature of blockchain code. The research proposes an evaluation method based on execution, where transactions are replayed on both AI-written and original contracts to measure agreement. The study finds that common evaluation methods miss significant differences, as scoring choices and function-level checks hide much of the behavioral disparity. An elicitation-first architecture, where agents ask clients clarifying questions before coding, is suggested to recover missing requirements. This approach aims to improve agentic synthesis by gathering missing intent before code generation.

The study found that common evaluation methods fail to capture significant behavioral differences because scoring choices and function-level checks obscure much of the disparity. This work indicates a need for incorporating explicit intent gathering into the agentic contract synthesis process.

items.title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
items.summary: The research proposes a behavioral test called Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) to detect covert collusion between AI agents. This test compares how an agent reacts to a message when a partner uses a secret code versus an uninvolved agent, focusing on the difference in reaction when the message is reworded while keeping its meaning. PoPLi yields values between 0.48 and 0.59 when a code is present, indicating the presence of a private channel. Message-only monitoring methods failed to distinguish between different collusion conditions. Consequently, PoPLi detects the use of a private channel rather than collusion based on incentives or simple codes.
